title: How to Speed Up Your Onboarding as an Engineering Leader
author: Karol Wojciszko
summary: Karol Wojciszko opens with the universal new-manager trap: every company has an unwritten engineering culture that new leaders discover only through a series of awkward, out-of-sync decisions, like rejecting a work-from-home request that every peer manager had already been quietly approving. His core reframe is that every incoming manager carries their own moral compass about how engineering teams should operate, and the first weeks on the job should be spent locating where the company's compass points before steering by one's own. Rather than asking the generic and useless 'what's the culture like here,' he prescribes a specific three-question calibration method for each of six named dimensions (Time Management and Trust, Growth and Development, Transparency, Flexible Work Time, Risk and Opportunity, and Decision-Making with the Team): ask for the negative limit (the worst thing the company has tolerated), the middle point (the default behavior), and the positive limit (the best thing that ever happened). The piece's sharpest insight is definitional: culture is determined by the worst thing an organization accepts, not the best thing it celebrates, which is why the negative-limit question is the one that actually reveals truth rather than aspiration. It closes with a maintenance warning: the managers who get burned aren't the ones who misread the culture on day one, but the ones who read it correctly once and never rechecked as the organization changed underneath them.
points: Reframes cultural onboarding as a compass-calibration problem: every new manager arrives with their own beliefs about how teams should operate, and the job of the first weeks is locating where the company's actual compass points before steering by one's own.

Replaces the generic, useless question 'what's the culture like here' with a structured three-point interview method (negative limit, middle point, positive limit) applied to six named dimensions including transparency, risk appetite, and flexible work time.

States the definitional insight driving the whole method explicitly: 'the level of culture is determined by the worst thing the company accepts,' not the best thing it publicly celebrates, making the negative-limit question the one that reveals ground truth.

Prescribes a concrete first-week action: schedule 30-minute conversations with the Head of Engineering, peer managers, and senior engineers, running the same three-question set across all six cultural dimensions to detect both consensus and disagreement.

Warns explicitly against treating the calibration as a one-time exercise, noting the managers who get burned are the ones who read the culture correctly on day one and never rechecked it as reorgs, new leadership, or bad quarters shifted the real floor.
quotes: Every company you join has an engineering culture. The problem is nobody writes it down. You discover it the hard way, one awkward decision at a time.

Here's something most new managers don't think about: you walk in with your own moral compass. The company has its own compass. And your job, especially in the first few weeks, is to figure out where theirs points before you start steering by yours.

For every dimension I care about, I ask three specific questions: The negative limit, the worst thing the company has accepted or done in this area. The middle point, the most common approach. The positive limit, the best thing that ever happened.

There's a definition I love that captures why the negative limit matters so much: The level of culture is determined by the worst thing the company accepts. Not the best thing they celebrate. The worst thing they tolerate.
The managers who get burned aren't the ones who read the culture wrong on day one. They're the ones who read it right on day one and never checked again.
